messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 49
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Architect
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 52

# Marcus

Marcus sits in the leather chair across from me with his hands folded in his lap, a habit he's developed over the past few weeks of our sessions. He's a tall man with salt-and-pepper hair, dressed in the kind of carefully considered casual wear that suggests someone accustomed to presenting himself professionally. His wife mentioned during the intake call that he hasn't been back to his architectural firm in three months.

Two years ago, Marcus was working on-site at a mixed-use development downtown, reviewing structural details with the general contractor. It was a Tuesday morning in late September. He was standing near the loading dock when a delivery truck's brakes failed. The driver, a man Marcus had spoken with several times over the project's duration, couldn't stop. Marcus watched from maybe thirty feet away as the truck struck a young laborer—couldn't have been more than twenty-five—pinning him against a steel beam. The image is still vivid in Marcus's mind: the shock on the man's face, the sounds, the terrible stillness afterward.

The paramedics arrived quickly. The laborer survived, though with severe injuries. But Marcus didn't witness the resolution. He left the site that day in a state of shock and never returned to that project.

For the first few months, Marcus told himself he was fine. He went back to his office, to his home office, drew plans, attended meetings. His wife, Jennifer, says he seemed distracted but functional. Then came October, and the anniversary of the incident approached. That's when the nightmares began—vivid, visceral replays where he's unable to warn the young man, unable to move, unable to stop what's coming. He wakes at three or four in the morning, his heart racing, drenched in sweat.

Now, whenever Marcus drives past construction sites, his chest tightens. He finds himself scanning for hazards, for things that could go wrong. When he's working on architectural designs, he gets stuck on safety details, reworking specifications obsessively. His colleagues have noticed. One asked if he was okay; another suggested he seemed "in his head" during a project review. Marcus knows they're right. He's become hypervigilant about structural safety in a way that's begun to paralyze his creative process.

The worst part, he tells me, is that he can't enjoy his work anymore. Architecture was never just a job for him—it was how he made meaning. He loved the problem-solving, the responsibility of creating spaces where people would live and work safely. Now, when he looks at his own designs, he sees only the ways they could fail, the catastrophes waiting to happen. He's turned down two promising projects in the past year because he couldn't shake the conviction that something would go wrong, that someone would get hurt because of a detail he'd missed.

His marriage has strained under the weight of it. Jennifer tries to be supportive, but Marcus has withdrawn. He doesn't want to talk about what happened. He's irritable in ways that surprise them both—snapping at her over small things, then feeling overwhelming guilt. Their intimacy has nearly disappeared. He lies awake beside her, ruminating, while she sleeps.

Marcus looks at his hands as he talks. He's intelligent, articulate, clearly trying to make sense of something that doesn't make sense. He keeps saying he should be fine, that he wasn't the one hurt, that he needs to just move past it. But his body hasn't gotten the message. His nervous system remains locked in that moment on the loading dock, scanning endlessly for the next disaster.
